title: HMS Alexander, 1794 — the captain who sent his friend away and fought five ships alone
sources: Wikipedia: Action of 6 November 1794 — HMS Alexander (Captain Richard Rodney Bligh) and HMS Canada (Captain Charles Hamilton), two 74-gun ships returning to Britain, were intercepted in the Celtic Sea by a French squadron under Contre-amiral Nielly: five 74-gun ships of the line plus frigates; the British watching force was absent at Plymouth; Nielly disguised his squadron's nationality to lure them close, then hoisted the French tricolour; Bligh ordered Hamilton to separate so he could escape without the slower Alexander; Canada outran the pursuit with no damage or casualties; Alexander was caught by several French ships in succession — the first two were driven off, Tigre lost her main and mizen topmasts; at 13:00, rigging and sails in tatters, masts shot through, hull shattered and fires burning, Bligh surrendered; Bligh estimated about 40 killed or wounded (French accounts: 28 killed, 30 wounded); a rare French victory between the Glorious First of June and the Battle of Groix

Wikipedia: HMS Alexander (1778) — Bligh was honourably acquitted by court martial on 27 May 1795; as the French Alexandre the ship was a poor sailor and at the Battle of Groix in June 1795 she was overrun by the British fleet and recaptured
Also on this day (candidates.md, in the app): 1217 Henry III issues the Charter of the Forest; 1917 Canadian forces capture Passendale

Paintings (public domain): William Shayer, HMS Alexander shortly before striking her colours, 6 November 1794 (1819); John Cleveley the Younger, the launch of HMS Alexander at Deptford, 1778; Lord Bridport's action off L'Orient (Groix), June 1795, paintings and prints; Thomas Luny, two ships hove to (illustrative); Julius Ibbetson, a storm (illustrative)
Illustrative stock footage (Pexels, free licence; not of the event): a stormy sea, a sailing ship's masts, rough water

post.facebook:
On this day in 1794, two British 74-gun ships, HMS Alexander and HMS Canada, sailing home through the Celtic Sea, ran into a trap.

At dawn a squadron appeared, disguised as British. Then it raised the French tricolour: five ships of the line under Admiral Nielly. Alexander was the slower ship, so her captain, Richard Rodney Bligh, ordered Canada to break away and save herself. Canada escaped without a scratch.

Alexander was caught. Bligh drove off the first French ship, then the second. By one o'clock his sails were in rags, his masts shot through, his hull shattered and fires burning below — and he surrendered.

A court martial honourably acquitted him. And seven months later, at the Battle of Groix, the British fleet overran the French Alexandre and took her back.

Also on 6 November: the Charter of the Forest (1217), and Canadian troops took Passendale (1917).

youtube.description:
6 November 1794: HMS Alexander and HMS Canada were sailing home when a squadron disguised as British raised the French flag — five ships of the line against two. Captain Richard Rodney Bligh ordered the faster Canada to escape, then fought on alone, driving off two French ships until his masts were shot through and fires burned below. He surrendered at one o'clock, was honourably acquitted — and seven months later the British recaptured his ship at the Battle of Groix.

Also on 6 November: the Charter of the Forest (1217) and Passchendaele (1917).
